assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework form the workhorse of modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice. Calvo's time-dependent price setting, Taylor's staggered contracts and interest-rate rule, and Woodford's integrated policy framework changed both theory and policy. Impact is very broad and durable, and it is directly relevant to the price-setting microfoundations literature.
assessment.attribution: The field has many contributors (Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others). Calvo (pricing mechanism), Taylor (contracts and policy rule) and Woodford (systematic normative theory) form the most defensible three-person core. Any three-person cut leaves out major contributors such as Gali, Gertler and the Christiano–Eichenbaum group.
assessment.maturity: Foundational work dates from the 1970s to the early 2000s and has been validated through decades of use. The Prize in 2022 went to banking and financial crises, not to this area, so the field has no overlapping recent award.
uncertainties: Attribution among Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali and Gertler is contestable.
Post-2008 and post-2021 inflation criticism of DSGE and New Keynesian models could weigh against it.
Overlap with the 2022 macro-finance award and the Heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian (HANK) successor literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation with random-coefficient discrete choice (BLP) and dynamic oligopoly models (Ericson–Pakes) are the empirical backbone of modern industrial organization. They are used constantly in merger review, antitrust and policy evaluation, and also in trade and other fields. The methodological advance is concrete and its influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: The BLP papers cleanly credit Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes also led the dynamic-games line, so his claim is the strongest. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are significant, and Bresnahan's claim as an empirical-IO pioneer is real. Leaving him out is a close call.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s and has been confirmed by three decades of broad application. Industrial organization has not been recognized since Tirole in 2014, and the structural empirical branch has never been recognized.
uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan should replace Levinsohn.
Possible concern that the contribution is mainly methodological or toolkit-oriented.
My own field proximity (industrial organization) could bias my judgment; I weigh it only through common criteria.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reoriented international trade theory and empirics. The Melitz (2003) model and the Helpman–Melitz–Yeaple work on exports versus foreign direct investment (FDI) explain facts about exporters and the gains from trade that earlier models missed. The agenda also shaped trade-policy analysis and data work.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's 2003 model is the central contribution and Helpman is the senior theorist who extended it widely, including HMY and later work on trade and inequality. Redding is a major contributor to quantitative trade but has a weaker claim to this specific discovery. Bernard, Jensen and Eaton–Kortum are important adjacent contributors who are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation and wide application. Trade has not been recognized since Krugman (2008), which strengthens the timing case.
uncertainties: Pareto-distribution and other functional-form assumptions drive the welfare conclusions.
Overlap with B011 and B044 in the trade field and with Helpman's other candidacy.
Credit for the empirical firm-level stylized facts (Bernard and Jensen) is not part of this ballot.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the measurement of local labour-market effects of import competition (the China shock) changed how economists and policymakers think about trade, automation and inequality. The influence on public debate and on research is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure across both the task-based and trade-shock lines. Hanson and Dorn are co-authors of the China shock work. Katz's earlier work on skill-biased change is important but is closer to the Autor–Katz–Kearney line. Acemoglu's task-based work was in part recognized in 2024, which complicates credit.
assessment.maturity: The China shock work dates from 2013 onward and the task framework from 2003 and later. Some follow-up evidence on persistence is still evolving.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2024 recognition of Acemoglu on institutions and technology.
Debate about the long-run magnitude of the shock and its interpretation.
Whether the committee prefers a more theoretical contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Historical and tax-record measurement of top income and wealth shares created a new empirical basis for inequality research and revived the field. The data and methods (World Inequality Database) are widely used and have influenced policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez established the top-incomes series, and Zucman extended it to offshore wealth and to distributional national accounts. Saez also appears in the optimal-taxation candidacy B014, so credit is spread across several overlapping ballots.
assessment.maturity: Core work from 2003 onward is well established as measurement. Theoretical claims in Capital in the Twenty-First Century (r > g) are more disputed, and measurement choices on wealth and capital are contested.
uncertainties: Controversy over methodology, data choices and the policy advocacy that accompanies the work.
Whether the committee judges the contribution as measurement rather than a causal or theoretical discovery.
Overlap of Saez with B014.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data used to measure intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and policy impacts opened a new empirical program with direct policy relevance. The method of linking tax records to outcomes has spread widely.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader. Hendren (neighbourhood causal effects) and Friedman (teacher value-added and tax-record work) are leading co-authors. Katz (Moving to Opportunity) is a significant contributor but is not selected here to keep the group small. Credit in a team-based research program is hard to divide.
assessment.maturity: Most key results date from 2014 onward and several are still being replicated or extended, so long-run confirmation is incomplete. The candidates are relatively young.
uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the program as mature enough.
Open questions on causal interpretation and replicability of place-based estimates.
Chetty also appears in B014, which spreads credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: GMM estimators for dynamic panel data (Arellano–Bond, Arellano–Bover, Blundell–Bond) are among the most widely used tools in applied microeconomics, macro-development and finance. The methods are cited extremely heavily and shaped practice.
assessment.attribution: The three credited names correspond to the core estimators. Hansen's earlier GMM work was recognized in 2013. Blundell has a large separate body of work in labour and consumption, so his claim rests on more than this ballot.
assessment.maturity: From the late 1980s to the late 1990s, with long confirmation. The contribution is also well understood in terms of limitations such as weak instruments and instrument proliferation.
uncertainties: Whether a purely methodological, tool-oriented contribution outranks substantive discoveries.
Known finite-sample problems with the estimators.
Competition from other econometrics candidacies.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Microfoundations and evidence on agglomeration, cities and housing explain productivity, wage and growth differences across places. Work on sources of agglomeration economies, the role of human capital in cities, and housing supply constraints is influential for policy. Krugman's 2008 prize covered theoretical economic geography but not this empirical and urban strand.
assessment.attribution: Duranton and Puga (microfoundations and the Handbook synthesis) and Glaeser (cities, human capital, housing) are the central names. Moretti and Gyourko are also strong, so the choice of three is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: Work extends from the 1990s to the present and is largely well established. Some recent strands, such as housing-supply regulation, are still being evaluated.
uncertainties: Credit division among at least five strong candidates.
Some of the contribution is a synthesis of ideas rather than a single discovery.
Some causal claims about agglomeration are hard to identify.
